### K08 — Propagation, geometry and physical transduction

**Canonical result:** phase/delay/Doppler and minimum vector field-to-port/sensor models, with bases, reference geometry, effective response, loading/coupling and cross-polar leakage. Derive the conditions for a scalar channel model. **Use/assessment:** calculate direction/frequency/polarization or sensor dependence and show which external-path changes internal injection cannot establish. **Limits:** narrowband/far-field/quasi-static assumptions, multipath, geometry and nuisance transduction. **Depth:** F minimum receiver model; S supporting fields/propagation; E full-wave radiators, detailed environments and specialist sensor laws. Externally supplied models must expose uncertainty and conventions.

### K09 — Physical disturbance generation and paths

**Canonical result:** convert physical thermal/representative active-device and external-field noise through loaded/coupled networks into delivered spectra and covariance. Develop reciprocal mixing with effective LO spectra, blocker/preselection/observation filtering and internal branch contributions; develop timing-error disturbance from the complete analog waveform and clock process. **Use/assessment:** calculate narrow-blocker/flat-spectrum limits and finite-spectrum contrasts; construct coupled covariance and derive filter/LO/clock constraints. **Limits:** source independence, impedance/power normalization, stationarity, small timing errors and unavailable physical parameters. **Depth:** F coherent source/path reasoning; S noise-network bridge; E detailed device physics and verified parameters. K13 assembles, rather than regenerates, these contributions.

### K10 — Detection, integration and signal-preserving rejection

**Canonical result:** correlation/matched filtering, applicable sufficient-statistic/likelihood reasoning, colored-noise weighting, coherent/noncoherent accumulation and reference mismatch. Develop separation/degree-of-freedom limits and effects of contaminated training or reference leakage. **Use/assessment:** realize and evaluate a bounded extraction/rejection method, calculating retained desired information, detection/correlation outcome and uncertainty. **Limits:** indistinguishable subspaces, finite support, covariance conditioning and pre-digital clipping. **Depth:** F coherent extraction/rejection; S general detection theory; E exhaustive adaptive/mission algorithms. Applications own their hypotheses, waveform mappings and task consequences.


### Chapter 8 — Fields, geometry and physical transduction

**Objective:** Construct the minimum physical input model and expose what receiver injection cannot establish.

**Entry:** Chapters 1 and 4 plus declared RF fields baseline; inference adds 5.

**Canonical ownership:** K08. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 8.1 Propagation and geometry

Develop phase/delay/Doppler and reference geometry, distinguishing propagation from electronic delay; identify multipath and near/far-field assumptions.

#### 8.2 Vector field to receiver ports

Bridge field/polarization bases, effective response, manifold, phase centers and loading/coupling. Keep the minimum receiver model internal.

#### 8.3 Scalar reduction and its failure

Derive conditions for scalar channels and quantify a direction/frequency/polarization mismatch; include cross-polar leakage and unobserved paths.

#### 8.4 Physical sensing interfaces

Develop representative transduction/reference paths and externally required laws with uncertainty. Detailed radiator synthesis, full-wave design and specialist sensor physics remain bounded external inputs.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** D-ARR compares electronic and field calibration; P-SEN separates measurand from nuisance. Specialist review must challenge scalar limits and interferometric geometry.

### Chapter 9 — Physical noise, blockers and timing disturbances

**Objective:** Construct physical spectra/covariance and derive constraints from the complete waveform.

**Entry:** Chapters 2–4 and RF noise/network baseline; incident fields add 8.

**Canonical ownership:** K09. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 9.1 Sources, loading and delivered noise

Bridge available/delivered power, temperature, thermal and representative active-device noise to network transfer with explicit impedances and normalization.

#### 9.2 Coupled and external noise

Construct covariance from loaded/coupled receiver and field paths rather than assume independent LNAs. Separate supplied parameters from derived relationships.

#### 9.3 Reciprocal mixing

Derive blocker/effective-LO contributions through preselection, mixer branches and observation filtering. Compare narrow-blocker/flat-spectrum limits with finite-spectrum cases.

#### 9.4 Timing-error generation

Derive small timing-error disturbance from the entire analog waveform and clock process, retaining correlations. Identify breakdown of tone-only, stationary and small-error models.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** X-BLK derives LO/clock/filter constraints; P-INT/D-ARR use physical covariance. Missing device evidence stays open; budget assembly belongs to Chapter 12.

### Chapter 10 — Extraction, integration and rejection

**Objective:** Derive a realizable extraction method and evaluate retained information.

**Entry:** Chapters 3–5; physical interference adds 8–9.

**Canonical ownership:** K10. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 10.1 Hypotheses and correlation

Develop representative likelihood/sufficient-statistic and matched-filter reasoning with explicit hypotheses and normalization.

#### 10.2 Colored weighting and accumulation

Derive coherent/noncoherent integration and mismatch consequences using Chapter 3 observation statistics, not a universal phase-loss rule.

#### 10.3 Separation and contaminated references

Develop spatial/spectral/temporal or reference-assisted rejection, degrees of freedom, training support, conditioning and leakage.

#### 10.4 Realizable decision and failure

Specify bounded extraction/rejection, false-alarm/detection conditions and retained wanted response. Digital realization follows later; analog survival must already be satisfied.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** D-COM and P-INT compare matched/mismatched extraction; X-INV tests indistinguishable subspaces. Apparent rejection alone is not improved task performance.

1	# Extraction, integration and rejection {#sec-extraction-rejection}
     2	
     3	A cancellation operation makes the output quieter. Has detection improved, or
     4	has the wanted signal been cancelled too? Answering requires a model for the
     5	observation, a decision rule and a calculation of the wanted transfer. Output
     6	noise power alone does not settle the question.
     7	
     8	We now join the physical response of [Chapter 8](fields-geometry-transduction.qmd)
     9	and the constructed disturbances of [Chapter 9](physical-disturbance-paths.qmd)
    10	to finite-record extraction. The reader should be able to derive a correlation
    11	statistic from explicit hypotheses, calculate false-alarm and detection
    12	probabilities, compare coherent and noncoherent integration, and reject an
    13	operation that removes wanted information. [Chapters 3–5](phase-delay-inference.qmd)
    14	supply observation statistics, conditioned linear algebra and inference. The
    15	new responsibility here is deciding what to retain when extracting or rejecting.
    16	All numerical inputs describe synthetic receivers, not measured performance.
    17	
    18	## Hypotheses, correlation and a decision {#sec-detection-correlation}
    19	
    20	Fix the receiver configuration, reference epoch, observation operator and valid
    21	acquisition state. Let $\mathbf x\in\mathbb C^M$ contain peak-scaled complex
    22	voltage observations after that operator: samples, channel outputs or selected
    23	linear coefficients. A known dimensionless template $\mathbf a$ contains its
    24	waveform, geometric response and calibrated phase orientation. It applies only
    25	over the stated band, geometry, loading and calibration history. Test
    26	
    27	$$
    28	 H_0:\ \mathbf x=\mathbf n,\qquad
    29	 H_1:\ \mathbf x=A\mathbf a+\mathbf n,
    30	$$
    31	
    32	where $A>0$ is a specified peak-voltage amplitude for the simple alternative.
    33	Assume centered, jointly proper complex Gaussian noise with known positive
    34	definite covariance $\mathbf C=E[\mathbf n\mathbf n^H]$ in V², identical under
    35	both hypotheses. “Proper” means the complementary covariance $E[\mathbf n\mathbf n^T]$
    36	vanishes; Gaussianity then supplies circular quadrature statistics. Chapter 9
    37	can construct $\mathbf C$, but neither a covariance nor a noise figure establishes
    38	the Gaussian distribution. Impulsive interference, clipping, uncertain covariance
    39	or signal-dependent noise requires another likelihood or a qualified detector.
    40	
    41	The interfaces need an explicit normalization. Chapter 8's field-to-voltage map
    42	has units metres when driven in V/m. Choose a specified nonzero reference
    43	responsivity in metres: its magnitude converts incident field amplitude to the
    44	voltage $A$, while the normalized dimensionless $\mathbf a$ retains relative
    45	channel, phase and waveform response. That reference is a model input or an
    46	external calibration result, not something electronic injection alone establishes.
    47	For stationary peak-envelope output noise with voltage spectral matrix
    48	$\mathbf S_z(\nu)$ from Chapter 9, define a row observation kernel
    49	$\mathbf b_i(t)$ in s⁻¹ acting on the centered output noise $\mathbf z_n(t)$:
    50	
    51	$$
    52	 n_i=\int \mathbf b_i(t)\mathbf z_n(t)\,dt,\qquad
    53	 \mathbf B_i(\nu)=\int \mathbf b_i(t)e^{+j2\pi\nu t}\,dt.
    54	$$
    55	
    56	The dimensionless $\mathbf B_i$ is the spectral row of this observation
    57	functional. Its plus sign follows by inserting inverse Fourier synthesis
    58	$e^{+j2\pi\nu t}$ for $\mathbf z_n(t)$; it is not the forward transform of
    59	$\mathbf b_i$. For example, sampling channel $k$ at $t_i$ gives
    60	$\mathbf B_i(\nu)=e^{+j2\pi\nu t_i}\mathbf e_k^T$, where $\mathbf e_k$ is
    61	the corresponding unit coordinate vector. Insert the spectral representation
    62	of $E[\mathbf z_n(t)\mathbf z_n(u)^H]$, with phase
    63	$e^{j2\pi\nu(t-u)}$, into $E[n_i n_j^*]$. Interchanging the convergent
    64	integrals gives one factor $\mathbf B_i$ and one $\mathbf B_j^H$:
    65	
    66	$$
    67	 C_{ij}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
    68	 \mathbf B_i(\nu)\mathbf S_z(\nu)\mathbf B_j(\nu)^H\,d\nu.
    69	$$
    70	
    71	The rows include finite windows, filtering and sample-time phases; the integral
    72	must converge. Its units are V². A white density is not a per-record variance,
    73	and shared paths or overlapping observations need not give independent records.
    74	Nonstationary disturbances require the covariance-kernel form of Chapter 3.
    75	These operations construct second moments, not the Gaussian law assumed above.
    76	
    77	Apply the **same observation** to the wanted voltage waveform. If before
    78	observation it is $\mathbf z_s(t)=A\mathbf p(t)$ with dimensionless
    79	$\mathbf p(t)$, then $a_i=\int\mathbf b_i(t)\mathbf p(t)\,dt$.
    80	Filtering only the noise model while keeping the original wanted template
    81	generally describes a different detector.
    82	
    83	For a concrete asymmetric example, let a proper stationary scalar voltage source
    84	$u(t)$ have density $S_0=1$ nV²/Hz on offsets $100\leq\nu\leq400$ Hz and zero
    85	elsewhere. Let $z_1(t)=u(t)$ and $z_2(t)=g u(t-d)$, where
    86	$g=0.7+j0.4$ and $d=0.7$ ms. Average channel 1 from 0.2 to 1.0 ms and channel 2
    87	from 2.0 to 3.3 ms. Write their starts $t_i$ and durations $T_i$; with
    88	$\operatorname{sinc}x=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$, the combined source-to-observation
    89	factors are
    90

## Vector field to receiver ports {#sec-field-ports}

Choose two real, orthonormal transverse basis vectors $\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2$
at each specified direction. The column $\mathbf E_\perp=(E_1,E_2)^T$ contains
complex electric-field components in V/m. A receiving linear structure maps
these components to open-circuit terminal voltages. Define its **receiving row**
$\mathbf h_i=(h_{i1},h_{i2})$, in metres, operationally by

$$
 v_{\mathrm{oc},i}=\mathbf h_i\mathbf E_\perp
 e^{jk_c\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf r_i},\qquad
 \mathbf v_{\rm oc}=\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\ell,f_c)\mathbf E_\perp.
$$

The spatial factor is included in row $i$ of $\mathbf H$ in the second expression.
This is a complex-linear receiving definition: the row times the field has no
additional conjugation. If a source instead specifies a polarization column
$\mathbf p_i$ by $v=\mathbf p_i^H\mathbf E_\perp$, our row is
$\mathbf h_i=\mathbf p_i^H$. Transmit-pattern conventions require their own
direction/basis translation. Hum's [receiving-antenna notes](https://www.waves.utoronto.ca/prof/svhum/ece422/notes/09a-receiving.pdf),
§3, motivate vector effective length and its voltage units; we define the receiving
row directly to avoid inheriting an ambiguous transmit/receive conjugation.

On rotating the transverse basis by a real orthogonal matrix $\mathbf U$, the
components become $\mathbf E'_\perp=\mathbf U^T\mathbf E_\perp$ and
$\mathbf H'=\mathbf H\mathbf U$. Thus $\mathbf H'\mathbf E'_\perp
=\mathbf H\mathbf E_\perp$: a coordinate change cannot change a terminal voltage.
A purported polarization model that fails this test has mixed conventions.

Effective response includes the installation, nearby structures and the other
antenna conductors in the specified open-circuit state. An isolated-element
pattern is not automatically an embedded array response. Likewise a phase centre
is a fitted geometric description over stated direction and frequency ranges,
not necessarily one immutable physical point. Moving a row's reference location
by $\delta\mathbf r$ requires multiplying its nonspatial response by
$\exp[-jk_c\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\delta\mathbf r]$ to preserve the same voltage.
The receiving manifold is the field-to-port matrix as a function of direction
and frequency. Only the complete manifold $\mathbf H$ is invariant to that bookkeeping choice.

 \mathbf v_L=\underbrace{\mathbf Z_L(\mathbf Z_A+\mathbf Z_L)^{-1}}_{\mathbf L}
 \mathbf v_{\rm oc},\qquad

small-signal operation and a fixed configuration. $\mathbf G$ maps the declared

## When a scalar channel is defensible {#sec-scalar-field-limit}

A scalar model can be exact for a restricted family of fields. If
$\mathbf E_\perp=\mathbf p\,s$, with fixed known polarization $\mathbf p$, then
$\mathbf z=\mathbf a s$, where $\mathbf a=\mathbf G\mathbf L\mathbf H\mathbf p$.
The scalar $s$ is a field amplitude in V/m if $\mathbf p$ is dimensionless; the
entries of $\mathbf a$ then have units metres. This reduction does not imply the
same $\mathbf a$ works at another direction, polarization, frequency or load.
For arbitrary incident polarizations, a fixed output-channel ratio exists only
when the corresponding rows of $\mathbf G\mathbf L\mathbf H$ are proportional
over the allowed input subspace. To see necessity, write the two response rows as $\mathbf m_1,\mathbf m_2$
and demand $z_2=\rho z_1$ for every allowed field. Then

input subspace. The rows restricted to that subspace must therefore be
proportional; conversely that proportionality gives the same ratio wherever
$z_1\ne0$. This is a rank condition on the orientation-normalized response,
not an electronics matching condition. Near a response null, even a small absolute discrepancy can
make the ratio and its phase unusable.

# Physical noise, blockers and timing disturbances {#sec-physical-disturbances}

A quiet terminated-input receiver can become noisy when an antenna, another
channel or a strong blocker is connected. Which physical source changed, and
through which path did its disturbance enter the reported observation? An
arbitrary covariance matrix cannot answer that question. Nor can a clock-jitter
number evaluated only at the wanted carrier.

This treatment constructs sources before combining them. The reader should be
able to convert thermal source voltage into delivered power, construct a coupled
noise matrix from a circuit or incident field, derive a blocker-dependent LO or
filter constraint, and test timing error against the complete analog waveform.
[Chapters 2–4](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) supply stochastic and matrix tools;
[Chapter 8](fields-geometry-transduction.qmd) supplies loaded field-to-port maps.
We use its fixed-configuration, orientation-normalized linear receiver interface.
All component values, spectra and targets below are synthetic teaching inputs.
None is a device guarantee or measured receiver result.

## Sources, loading and delivered noise {#sec-loaded-noise}

Keep two representations distinct. For a real centered stationary voltage $e(t)$,
use two-sided $S_e(f)$ over signed physical frequency $f$, in V²/Hz, with
$E[e^2]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_e(f)\,df$. A resistor $R$ at temperature $T$
has the classical open-circuit thermal model

$$
 S_e(f)=2k_BT R,
$$

over a finite band where resistance is approximately real, equilibrium holds and
$h_P|f|\ll k_BT$. Here $k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant
and $h_P$ denotes Planck's constant. The classical model is not extended to
infinite bandwidth. Analog Devices [MT-047](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-047.pdf),

## Coupled networks and external fields {#sec-physical-covariance}

Stack physical source amplitudes into $\mathbf u$, give their cross-spectral
matrix $\mathbf S_u$, and solve the loaded circuit to obtain $\mathbf n=\mathbf T\mathbf u$.
Then

$$
 \mathbf S_n=\mathbf T\mathbf S_u\mathbf T^H.
$$

Chapter 4 owns this propagation identity. The engineering work here is deciding
what $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf T$ physically contain. A common source uses one
column reaching multiple outputs. Mutually independent local sources have a
diagonal source matrix, but a nondiagonal transfer can still correlate outputs.
Conversely, device-internal source correlations belong in $\mathbf S_u$.

External fields enter through the same receiving manifold as wanted fields.
For finitely many angular/polarization patches $\alpha$ with mutually uncorrelated
centered peak-scaled complex field-envelope vectors and matrices $\mathbf F_\alpha(\nu)$
in (V/m)²/Hz at offset $\nu$ from the positive RF carrier,

$$
 \mathbf S_{\rm field}=\sum_\alpha

$$

at the output $\mathbf z$ plane after $\mathbf G$; every transfer is evaluated
at physical frequency $f_c+\nu$. To combine it with the resistor example, first
translate its real two-sided loaded matrix to $4\mathbf S_L(f_c+\nu)$, then
propagate through the same electronics. Do not add the two representations

independence is an assumption; coherent reflections of the **same** source must
be summed as transfer paths before forming its outer product. For one scalar

that path. Noise sources representing the same passive loss or thermal field
must not be counted twice. Actual arrays require measured or independently
supported impedance, embedded response, environment and active-noise parameters.

## Define the operator before integrating noise

Let phi(t) be a real, centered residual phase in radians, after explicitly separating
deterministic mean phase, drift and spurs. Assume wide-sense stationarity and finite
variance where a stationary spectrum is used. Write R(tau)=E[phi(t+tau)phi(t)].
Our local Fourier convention is

$$
 S(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} R(\tau)e^{-j2\pi f\tau}\,d\tau,
 \qquad R(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S(f)e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,df.
$$

Here f is offset frequency in Hz and S is a two-sided phase density in rad²/Hz.
We restrict ordinary integrals to models for which the transforms and weighted
integrals exist; spectral lines and nonstationary models need separate treatment.

The relationship between correlation, spectral density and LTI weighting is also
developed in Oppenheim and Verghese, Chapter 10, equations (10.1)–(10.3)
([MIT text](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-011-introduction-to-communication-control-and-signal-processing-spring-2010/8075041184d566103ce7c3f69afc5e75_MIT6_011S10_chap10.pdf)).

$$
 \operatorname{var}q=\iint w(t)w(s)R(t-s)\,dt\,ds

$$

The second equality follows by inserting the inverse transform and collecting
the t and s integrals; exchanging integrals requires convergence. A normalized
average has w=1/T on [0,T] and zero elsewhere, so
W=exp(-j pi f T) sinc(fT), where sinc(x)=sin(pi x)/(pi x). The variance is
therefore weighted by sinc²(fT), not by a sharp frequency cutoff at 1/T.

followed by angle extraction: a weighted sum of phasors and a weighted sum of
angles generally differ. For phases 0 and pi/2, weights 3/4 and 1/4 give
arg(3/4+j/4)=0.321751 rad versus the weighted angle pi/8=0.392699 rad. Sampled data also
